data.title: OrbiMed Advisors Discloses Investment at Aspen Neuroscience, Inc. with 12.3% Stake
data.description:
OrbiMed Advisors Discloses Investment at Aspen Neuroscience, Inc. with 12.3% Stake

OrbiMed Advisors LLC, a registered investment adviser, reported beneficial ownership of 12.3% of Aspen Neuroscience, Inc.’s common stock, held through OrbiMed Private Investments VII, LP. In its Nov. 6, 2026, Schedule 13D, the firm said the fund acquired the shares through preferred-stock conversions tied to Aspen’s IPO and a purchase of 1 million IPO shares at $15 each. OrbiMed said it made the investment for financial purposes, not to take control of Aspen.

Investor Intent

OrbiMed Advisors said it bought the shares as an investment, not to control Aspen Neuroscience. It reported no current proposals for a merger, asset sale, board or management change, or other major corporate change.

Investor's Background

OrbiMed Advisors LLC is a Delaware limited liability company and a registered investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act. It serves as managing member of OrbiMed Capital GP VII LLC, which is general partner of OPI VII, the limited partnership that holds the Aspen shares. Through those roles, OrbiMed Advisors shares authority to vote and dispose of the fund’s holdings.

Original SEC Filing: Aspen Neuroscience, Inc. [ ASPE ] - SCHEDULE 13D - Nov. 06, 2026

data.title: AMTD Group Discloses 95.7% Stake in The Generation Essentials Group
data.description:
AMTD Group Discloses 95.7% Stake in The Generation Essentials Group

AMTD Group Inc., through AMTD IDEA Group and AMTD Digital Inc., disclosed beneficial ownership of 95.7% of The Generation Essentials Group’s ordinary shares. On Nov. 2, 2026, its subsidiary AMTD Digital received 198,630,381 newly issued Class A shares in exchange for hotel assets valued at $209.8 million. The deal gives AMTD Group 96.7% of the ordinary shares’ voting power and prompted the group to move from passive Schedule 13G reporting to Schedule 13D.

Investor Intent

AMTD Group says it has no current plan to acquire more shares beyond the hotel-asset transaction. It says it will review its holdings regularly and could later buy or sell shares or pursue other steps, but it names no specific additional action.

Investor's Background

AMTD Group Inc. is a British Virgin Islands company whose business portfolio spans financial services, digital solutions, media and culture, education and training, and premium assets and hospitality. The group describes itself as a conglomerate with businesses across these sectors. AMTD Group controls AMTD IDEA Group, which controls AMTD Digital Inc.

Original SEC Filing: Generation Essentials Group [ TGE ] - SCHEDULE 13D - Nov. 06, 2026

data.title: Axalta-Akzo Nobel merger conditionally approved by European Union
data.description:
The European Union said Friday it conditionally approved the proposed all-stock merger of Axalta Coating Systems and Akzo Nobel after the companies agreed to sell assets in ‌Europe to address competition concerns.

The European Commission - the European Union's competition authority - said on Friday that the groups would divest Akzo Nobel's vehicle refinish coatings business in Europe to a suitable buyer to address ​concerns over the merged company's strong market power that ​could lead to price hikes for repair garages and consumers.

The merger will create a global coatings company with ~$17B in revenue and a broad portfolio across Powder Coatings, Aerospace Coatings, Refinish, Mobility, Marine and Protective Coatings, Industrial Coatings, and Decorative Coatings.

"Receiving the European Commission's approval is an important milestone as we move closer to completing our merger with Axalta," said Greg Poux-Guillaume, AkzoNobel CEO, who will become CEO of the combined company.

data.title: The Wild Week That Brought AI Investors to the Brink — WSJ
data.description:
By Hannah Erin Lang, Sam Goldfarb and Gunjan Banerji

Ben Emons can pinpoint almost exactly when the first wave of the midterm elections crashed over Wall Street.

Emons, whose firm provides investment research, was sitting at his downtown Manhattan office at 9 p.m. on Tuesday when his Android phone started ringing. It didn't stop until midnight. He tried to stay awake between calls by doing push-ups on the floor next to his desk. Some clients couldn't believe what was unfolding — or fathom what the Democrats' landslide might mean for the market, he said. "People were caught off guard," Emons said. "This is a real shock event."

"I cannot see this working," one of them sighed. "At all."

Markets often react, and sometimes overreact, to surprises. But Tuesday's election sent Wall Street into a tizzy of historic proportions; stocks rocked violently in the three days that followed, as the Democrats' victories supercharged anxieties over an artificial-intelligence trade that had been building for weeks.

The reckoning came on Thursday, when AI darlings Nvidia and Micron Technology helped lead the Nasdaq composite into correction territory. Hedge funds dumped positions. The Cboe Volatility Index or VIX, known as Wall Street's "fear gauge," jumped to its highest level since March.

For weeks, investors had fretted over the piles of debt on data-center operators' balance sheets, the shrinking cash reserves at tech giants such as Alphabet, and the sneaking suspicion that the AI ecosystem's peak profits were already in the past. Few, though, expected Democrats to win gubernatorial races in states like Texas, Ohio and Georgia that have emerged as key battlegrounds over future data-center projects.

The week was marked by haywire trading: Markets reacted positively to the election news at first, sending blue-chip stocks to their best day in months.

The relief was short-lived. Wednesday's rally gave way to a punishing Thursday selloff that erased $2.5 trillion in market value from the Nasdaq composite and dragged major indexes to their biggest one-day drop since the "Liberation Day" drop in April 2025.

Now investors are left to grapple with the question of whether this is another stretch of choppy trading or the early unwinding of the stock market's all-consuming, massive bet on the technological revolution.

"A slowing of growth for AI stocks seems inevitable," said Timothy Casaletto, an equity portfolio manager at Wellington Management. "The speed of the build-out is more likely than not to be slower than the market previously anticipated."

Heading into Tuesday night, most Americans had far-bigger concerns than the fate of a data-center development in rural Texas.

As the evening's first results trickled in, stock-index futures initially slipped. They reversed after the decisiveness of the victories became clear and President Trump gave interviews saying he accepted the election results.

George Mateyo, chief investment officer at Key Private Bank, was watching the results at home, texting with work colleagues, when he read the news about Trump's remarks. They mattered, Mateyo thought.

"The notion that we would see a real contested, nasty, contentious type of period of time, that risk had gone down," he said. "I felt positive about that."

Wall Street's good mood extended through Wednesday. Shares of "real-economy" companies like home builders and major retailers surged. The Dow industrials logged their best day since April — and for a moment, it looked like traders were mostly relieved that the election was over.

Wednesday's rally proved something of a headfake.

When Kevin Xu, an investor and content creator, glanced at the stock market prices at about 10:30 a.m. ET Thursday, he did a double-take. His first thought: "I hope this is a mistake."

The San Francisco-based content creator was staring at a 4% drop in the Nasdaq that had erased a six-figure sum from his retirement portfolio practically overnight. Across his social-media feeds, other individual investors were in various states of denial. Or duress. Some posted memes and all-caps rants. One posted the phone number for a mental-health hotline.

"There's nothing to do," he said of the drop. "You just watch."

There was no midday relief. The waves of selling in the U.S. stock market accelerated as the day wore on. Traders were getting jumpy; Wall Street's "fear gauge" VIX spiked.

Systematic trades helped amplify the losses. That jump in the VIX potentially triggered a group of funds known as volatility-control funds, which tend to make buying and selling decisions based on the level of turbulence in markets, to start dumping stocks. They added to an avalanche of selling, joining hedge-fund firms, rookie investors and other money managers.

Barclays estimates that volatility-control funds slashed their exposure to the stock market by 30 percentage points, the biggest one-day decline since February 2020, when the Covid-19 pandemic jolted markets.

By 3 p.m., with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down around 4.5%, some traders were peering at their screens and wondering if things would turn around, as they sometimes have in the final hour before the closing bell. Instead, the selloff worsened.

Some newfangled trades may have exacerbated the moves. Traders pointed to the billions of dollars sitting in leveraged exchange-traded products, which turbocharge exposure to the stock market. Assets in these funds have been at highs this year, and their rebalancing activity around the market close can fuel more volatility.

Several traders said Thursday's selloff was a classic example of a crowded trade unraveling, and the moves were driven by positioning across markets.

The market was "puking anything related to AI," Wellington's Casaletto said.

Instead of the YOLO bets that would pay out if AI and chip stocks kept surging, traders piled into bets that would profit from a market crash. Total options volumes hit the highest level on record in data going back to the 1970s.

Cem Karsan, a volatility manager and founder of Kai Wealth, said he has purchased complex derivatives — including those tied to the VIX, options tied to the S&P 500 and credit-default swaps in the bond market — that would pay out if volatility surged. He is bracing for more market tumult in coming months.

"This is an incredibly dangerous couple of days for the market," Karsan said.

Tech stocks staged a partial recovery on Friday, though all major U.S. indexes still ended the week in the red.

One key question is whether the momentum behind the AI trade will shift into a lower gear moving forward. The buy-it-all investing boom that characterized the early years of the bull market for tech stocks is petering out, analysts said. And a new phase is under way.

"This is what happens: we shift into a more sustainable velocity for the economy and for earnings," said Dan Farley, the chief investment officer for U.S. Bank Asset Management Group. "But there's turbulence when you shift from one speed to another."

Key Private Bank's Mateyo said his team has started to think about looking for buying opportunities, seeing the election as more of "a rebuke of the current political status quo" than it was a "rebuke of the economic and financial status quo."

State-level rules will likely slow — but not stop — data-center construction, he added. The public might have some qualms about AI, but over time, people will continue to "use it, incorporate it into their work, into their lives, and some of that cynicism or skepticism might fade over time."

Some investors aren't so sure Americans will learn to love data centers as neighbors.

"What we got out of the election was quantifiable evidence that there is real disdain for the data-center build-out," said Matt Rowe, senior portfolio manager at Man Group. Americans voted so overwhelmingly against data centers in local ballot measures that it "started to change my mindset around the probability of these projects getting executed," he said.

"All else equal, these projects are going to take longer to get executed, and they're going to cost more to do."

data.title: A Berkshire Hathaway Electric Utility Wants a Historic Rate Hike in California — WSJ
data.description:
By Jennifer Hiller

A California electric utility owned by Berkshire Hathaway is asking regulators for a rate increase that would boost the typical residential bill by $120 a month, a stunning request even in an era of rising electricity costs.

Pacific Power, part of Berkshire-owned PacifiCorp, faces a costly problem: It has a small rural customer base to share the expense of hardening the power grid in a sprawling, wildfire-prone area of Northern California.

"It's a rugged territory; it's densely forested; it's dry," said President Ryan Flynn. "We have about four customers per square mile."

The utility on Friday asked state regulators to approve a 57% rate increase — one of the largest-ever such requests by an investor-owned U.S. utility — that would boost its base revenue by $103 million a year.

Pacific Power's filing highlights a deepening dilemma across the American West as utilities boost spending to try to avoid catastrophic wildfires while debating with regulators over how customers and shareholders should share costs for past disasters.

The utility's equipment has allegedly been tied to two blazes in California: the 2020 Slater Fire that burned more than 150,000 acres and killed two people and the 2022 McKinney Fire that burned 60,000 acres and killed four.

Much of the requested $103 million reflects capital spending already under way to safeguard the grid.

Flynn said the company is swapping wooden power poles for steel and fiberglass structures and replacing hundreds of miles of bare wire with insulated, fire-resistant conductor. The utility also faces steep increases in insurance premiums and general operational inflation.

Pacific Power's Northern California territory sweeps across 11,292 square miles from the coast to the Nevada border, serving about 46,000 customers. It also operates in Oregon, where it has far more customers: about 630,000.

Beyond the rate case, Pacific Power faces about $637 million in liability claims and legal expenses stemming from the 2020 and 2022 fires. It is asking regulators to let it recover $340.5 million of that sum from customers. It disputes responsibility for the blazes but has settled claims nonetheless.

If the request is approved, the average monthly residential bill for most customers would increase by an additional $46, or about 19%, the company has said. It plans to ask for approval to securitize those costs, a strategy utilities often use for storm or fire recovery, which could lessen the bill impact by spreading out payments over a long period.

Regulators will consider both proposals in 2027 — they previously approved a 24.4% rate increase that took effect in 2024.

One potential offset: Consumers could see relief on fuel and power adjustments early next year that could trim their electric bills by about $31 a month, or 14%, according to Pacific Power.

"We recognize the magnitude of this request, and protecting communities is the right thing to do. Doing nothing is not an option," said Flynn, who called the requests "the beginning of a process."

The debate over wildlife liability costs remains contentious in California, where a bid by Gov. Gavin Newsom to reduce utilities' exposure recently failed in the state legislature.

Electricity-cost increases are outpacing many other types of inflation across the U.S. and straining the wallets of Americans facing higher food and gasoline costs as well.

Already, about one-third of Pacific Power's California customers receive utility discounts under the state's low-income energy assistance program.

Through September, utilities have requested more than $23 billion in rate increases this year, according to data tracked by PowerLines, a consumer education group. In 2025, they asked for $31 billion.

Pacific Power's rate-hike requests outpace much of the rest of the industry. In the past two years, some of the highest requests have ranged from 12% to the high 20% range, according to PowerLines.

One of the largest came in 2024 from another unit of PacifiCorp — Rocky Mountain Power initially proposed a 29% rate increase that Utah Gov. Spencer Cox on X called "laughable if it wasn't so dangerous."

The utility lowered its request and ultimately received a rate bump of about 4% following a settlement earlier this year.

In 2024, Warren Buffett warned shareholders that Berkshire might rethink utility investments in states at high risk of wildfire.

"We will not knowingly throw good money after bad," he wrote in his annual letter.

A representative for Berkshire Hathaway didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

PacifiCorp has halted dividend payments to Berkshire and agreed earlier this year to sell much of its Washington service area, power generation and infrastructure to Portland General Electric for $1.9 billion to raise capital. S&P has lowered PacifiCorp's issuer credit rating to BBB-minus, the lowest investment grade rating.

Write to Jennifer Hiller at jennifer.hiller@wsj.com

Howard have resigned as directors of the Company, and that Kevin Ma and Brett Halvorson have been appointed to the board of directors, effective November 5, 2026. Mr. Howard will continue as Vice President, Exploration of the Company.

“On behalf of the board, I would like to thank Dominic and Avrom for their contributions as directors, including their guidance through the completion of our transaction and listing on the CSE. We are pleased that Avrom will continue to lead our exploration work at Liberty Ridge, and we welcome Kevin and Brett to the board.”, said Fiona Keating, Chief Executive Officer of the Company.

Kevin Ma

Kevin Ma, CPA, CA, is the Principal of Calibre Capital Partners Corp., a firm specializing in corporate finance advisory and corporate services. With more than 20 years of experience in financial management and public company operations, Mr. Ma is a Chartered Professional Accountant holding a Bachelor of Arts from the University of British Columbia and a Diploma in Accounting from the Sauder School of Business at the University of British Columbia. He currently serves as an officer and/or director for several publicly listed and private companies within Calibre Capital’s client portfolio.

Brett Halvorson

Mr. Halvorson brings 15+ years of expertise in corporate finance, capital strategy, and financial operations across the agriculture, mining, and technology sectors. Currently, as the Chief Financial Officer of Virtuo, he leads financial planning and reporting, capital allocation, and strategic financial governance. His experience includes structuring complex financial frameworks, sourcing and deploying capital across multi-sector organizations, raising institutional capital, and establishing disciplined long-term financial strategy. Mr. Halvorson holds a Bachelor of Commerce from the University of Alberta and is a CFA Charterholder.

Following these changes, the board of directors of the Company consists of Fiona Keating, Ryan Cheung, Jason Latkowcer, Kevin Ma and Brett Halvorson, and the audit committee consists of Jason Latkowcer (Chair), Kevin Ma and Fiona Keating.

About Tungsten Eagle Development Corp.

Tungsten Eagle Development Corp. is a Canadian company focused on tungsten exploration at its Liberty Ridge property in Elko County, northeastern Nevada. The property comprises approximately 5,351 acres (2,165.5 hectares) and includes the site of the historical Mitchell silver mine.

data.title: Research Reports — Barrons.com
data.description:
These reports, excerpted and edited by Barron's, were issued recently by investment and research firms. The reports are a sampling of analysts' thinking; they should not be considered the views or recommendations of Barron's. Some of the reports' issuers have provided, or hope to provide, investment-banking or other services to the companies being analyzed.

Datadog — DDOG-Nasdaq Outperform — $220.52 on Nov. 4 by Evercore ISI Even though Datadog stock was down 22% since the last call, the bar was still high heading into the quarter, as shares are up 62% year to date and a clean "beat and raise" was needed. Datadog delivered a solid about 5% beat (vs. last-12-months average of 4.6%), but the company only guided to estimated fourth-quarter 2026 revenue growth of about 25% at the midpoint, falling short of our 29% walk-up estimate, causing shares to sell off by about 19% premarket.

As far as the results go, Datadog delivered a strong fiscal third quarter highlighted by revenue of $1.2 billion (+35%), slightly decelerating from 36% in the prior quarter but well above management guidance of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion (+28%-29%) and our/Street estimates of $1.140 billion/$1.146 billion. This equated to a 5% beat, above the 4.3% beat last quarter but slightly below the 5.3% beat in first-quarter 2026, which we think was fine.

Operating margins of 26.1% were above our forecast of 23.3% and Street estimates of 23.5%, which speaks to the company's ability to drive operating leverage even as it invests to drive further growth.

Navitas Semiconductor — NVTS-Nasdaq Buy — $8.56 on Nov. 4 by Needham Navitas Semiconductor reported third-quarter 2026 results and fourth-quarter 2026 guidance that came ahead of Street expectations, driven by high-power end markets. Our key takeaways include: 1) Revenue from high-power end markets grew 50% quarter over quarter and triple digits Y/Y. Visibility is improving, as book-to-bill was well above 1.0 and backlog is extending into mid-2027. Heading into fiscal-year 2027, Navitas expects double-digit percentage revenue growth Q/Q throughout the year, with an acceleration in second-half 2027. 2) The acquisition of Claros positions Navitas with a power portfolio that spans from the grid to the xPU. 3) The company's AI infrastructure segment...is forecast to triple Y/Y in fiscal 2027, driven by the transition to 800V DC architectures. We reiterate our Buy rating but lower our target price to $15, reflecting multiple compression across the broader industry.

Owens Corning — OC-NYSE Hold — $117.76 on Nov. 4 by StoneX Research Owens Corning reported softer-than-anticipated third-quarter 2026 results recently as persistently challenging residential market conditions, weak storm activity, and rapidly rising transportation and input material costs led to an across-the-board miss of Street estimates.

While it was expected to be a challenging quarter (third-quarter 2026 Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association industry shipments down about 13% year over year and total housing starts down about 4% Y/Y), there was optimism for the company's largest segment to outperform the broader market, given the location of some more significant summer storms; ultimately, that was not the case, with Roofing coming in about 16% lower Y/Y. With the storm and build seasons in the rearview mirror, management expects to see a continuation of current market conditions likely to result in channel destocking as we head into year end.

Resolve Group — RVLV-NYSE Buy — $21.53 on Nov. 4 by TD Cowen For the next-gen fashion retailer and lifestyle brand focused on Millennial and Gen Z consumers, third-quarter top-line growth impressed at 20% Y/Y, but fourth-quarter implied Ebitda margin guide was below Street, driven by continued investment and elevated freight costs. October growth has moderated to the midteens, with tougher compares ahead in November/December. Still, we see potential upside to holiday expectations, as improving brand resonance and higher marketing spend could support stronger-than-expected demand. Target price: $25.

CarMax — KMX-NYSE Neutral — $53.38 on Nov. 3 by Seaport Research Partners The CarMax executive team recently revealed its Shift Into GEAR Strategy. In brief terms, the company plans to reduce costs and operate more efficiently, investing the savings in pricing in order to drive more consistent unit sales growth, which should drive operating leverage and consequently earnings growth. It was very consistent with how the company has been speaking in recent quarters since the arrival of new CEO Keith Barr (now seven months on the job)....

We are encouraged by the company's financial/CAGR targets for fiscal 2026-fiscal 2030 and believe the plan is both logical and sensible and that the growth targets are achievable....Given the company's earnings track record in recent years, midteens earnings-per-share growth is certainly a big improvement — rough calculations assuming the midpoint implies EPS just under $5 for fiscal 2030. Ascribing a 20 times multiple to that and discounting back three years at 10% suggests a valuation of about $70 per share — 33% upside compared with today's close....

We are encouraged by the Shift Into GEAR strategy and the corresponding financial targets....That said, there is still execution risk — so until tangible progress is evident, we wait on the sidelines.
